endorsements.quote: When institutions provide no governed pathway, clinicians improvise, already using consumer-grade frontier models for documentation, differentials, and patient communication without oversight ( 10 – 12 ).

The clinician-builder should be fluent enough in implementation and regulatory science to help specify, with the institutional AI center, the elements that determine what is built and how success is judged: intended use and user population, risk classification ( 17 ), the evidence and validation plan ( 18 ), human-oversight provisions, and lifecycle governance—model registration, safety thresholds, monitoring cadence, rollback, and sunset criteria ( 19 , 20 ).

unlisted_practices: Recognize and support the clinician-builder role, a frontline clinician who identifies workflow failures and prototypes AI tools, within institutions.

Form formal partnerships in which clinician-builders define and prototype tools while AI centers and co-equal experts in data science, software engineering, human factors, and ethics harden, govern, and scale them.
Accept validated clinical AI tools as scholarship in training and pair this with foundational competencies in AI literacy, data governance, and implementation and regulatory science.
Adopt intellectual property policy that distinguishes clinician-built clinical software from biotechnology licensing.
Provide a secure sandbox with de-identified data for clinician prototyping and prohibit protected data in consumer AI tools.
Prioritize pediatric critical care as an early setting for rigorous evaluation of clinical AI and do not export models that fail there without reexamination.
Ensure clinician-builders remain clinically active to sustain bedside engagement.

screen.reason: This is a commentary advocating for the role of the clinician-builder in developing and governing bedside AI in the pediatric intensive care unit.
